summary: Gives an overview and rationale of the architecture for securing data sent to large multicast groups. It introduces a multicast security reference framework and identifies the security services that a solution might include. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When one person sends the same message to a huge crowd, how do you keep outsiders from reading it? This is the big-picture plan.

questions: what is multicast group security architecture
what is a group security association
what is a gcks in multicast security
subtitle: A framework for securing data sent to large multicast groups: who holds keys, who sets policy, and which security associations tie it together.

tldr.problem: Securing IP multicast group communication is complex, so a secure multicast protocol suite needs several functional areas that address different aspects.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Reference Framework with three functional areas (data handling, group key management, security policies), the Group Controller/Key Server, Sender, Receiver and Policy Server entities, and the Group Security Association (GSA) made of REG, REKEY and DATA SAs.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational architecture that names the security services a solution might include; algorithms and protocols are left to other work, such as the Group Domain of Interpretation.

today: RFC 3740 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the architecture overview for multicast group security, and its group key management ideas appear in protocols such as RFC 3547.

sections.title: Scope and Audience
sections.content:
RFC 3740 describes the functional areas of a secure IP multicast protocol suite and how they relate. The architecture is aimed at large multicast groups. It can be used for smaller groups, but the RFC says it is not necessarily the most efficient means, and that other architectures such as Cliques can be more efficient for small ad-hoc groups.

The architecture is end to end. It does not require multicast routing protocols (such as PIM) or admission control protocols (such as IGMP and MLD) to take part, so joining a secure group is independent of joining an IP multicast group. It does not describe how secure groups deal with NAT, and it does not require reliable mechanisms. The audience is the technical community and implementers who already know IP and IPsec.
sections.eli5: This plan is for big crowds, not a few friends. It works on its own, without needing the network's help to keep secrets.

sections.title: The Multicast Security Reference Framework
sections.content:
The Reference Framework organizes the architecture into three functional areas and shows entities as boxes and interfaces as arrows. A box means a function, not necessarily one physical machine, and an implementation may merge several boxes.

In the centralized design there are four kinds of entity. The Group Controller and Key Server (GCKS) issues and manages keys and checks authentication and authorization of candidate members. The Sender transmits to the group: one in a 1-to-N group, two or more in an M-to-N group. The Receiver gets the data. The Policy Server creates and manages group security policies and talks to the GCKS. Senders and Receivers both interact with the GCKS for key management.

A distributed design extends this for very large groups. GCKS entities talk to other GCKS entities, and Policy Servers to each other, and they must authenticate and securely interact with peers. All Receivers must obtain identical keys and policy.
sections.eli5: Think of a club. One person hands out membership keys, another writes the club rules, and members either speak or listen. A huge club can have several key-keepers who cooperate.

sections.title: The Three Functional Areas
sections.content:
Multicast data handling covers how data is treated at sender and receiver. Data is typically encrypted with the group key, mainly for access control and possibly for confidentiality, and authenticated. Source authentication and integrity guarantee the data came from the claimed source and was not modified, while group authentication only shows it came from some group member. Source authentication needs special-purpose transforms; the RFC points to Multicast ESP and the TESLA algorithm, while encryption and group authentication can use off-the-shelf solutions.

Group key management is the secure distribution and refreshment of keying material. It includes member authentication, secure channels to and between GCKS entities, changing keys, and detecting key compromise. The Group Domain of Interpretation (RFC 3547), GSAKMP and MIKEY are named as instances.

Multicast security policies must also describe how the group is governed, such as the authorization level to join, when a member is forcibly removed, and how to resynchronize after lost key messages. Policy creation, translation and negotiation are harder because groups span several administrative domains.
sections.eli5: There are three jobs: protect the messages, manage the keys, and write the rules. Each job needs its own helpers, but they must work together.

sections.title: Group Security Associations
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a set of policy and cryptographic keys that provide security services to matching traffic. A Group Security Association (GSA) is the multicast counterpart. It is both a superset of an SA, adding group policy attributes such as credentials needed to join and whether to re-key when members are added (backward re-key) or removed (forward re-key), and an aggregation of several SAs.

Three categories of SA can make up a GSA.

  • Registration SA (REG): a unicast SA between the GCKS and each member. The member initiates it to pull GSA information, and it protects the other SAs. It may be set up manually, for example on a smart card.
  • Re-key SA (REKEY): a single multicast SA from the GCKS to all members, used to push new SAs or quickly revoke members. It is not negotiated and is not absolutely required.
  • Data Security SA (DATA): a multicast SA protecting data from senders to receivers. It is not negotiated; members obtain it from the GCKS. There may be one per sender, one for the whole group, or a mix.

Compositions vary: memory-constrained members may need only REG and one DATA SA; a pay-per-session group may need no REKEY SA; a subscription group needs REG and REKEY to refresh the DATA SA when membership changes.
sections.eli5: A club has three kinds of secrets: a private one between you and the key-keeper, a shared one the key-keeper uses to announce changes, and a shared one everyone uses to read the club's messages.

sections.title: Security Services
sections.content:
The RFC assigns six security services to the framework's interfaces, without analyzing trust, performance or algorithms.

  • Data confidentiality: encrypting at the sender and decrypting at the receiver. Because multicast traffic is usually connectionless UDP, stream ciphers may be unsuitable.
  • Source authentication and data integrity: one of the harder areas, because of connectionless and real-time requirements.
  • Group authentication: only shows a group member sent the data, but is simple and efficient, and gives a weak integrity check useful against denial of service.
  • Group membership management: registration and de-registration with the Group Controller, independent of IGMP or MLD joins and leaves.
  • Key management: distributing and updating keying material over the group's life. ISAKMP is noted as extensible to multicast key management.
  • Policy management: policy definitions, the Policy Server, and its communication with the Key Server, possibly using a policy infrastructure such as COPS.
sections.eli5: Six services keep the club safe: scrambling messages, proving who sent them, proving the sender is a member, signing people up and out, handing out new keys, and keeping the rules straight.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework is end to end and does not rely on the network between group controllers and members. It does not address denial of service, message deletion or other active attacks on unicast or multicast routing, or on admission control protocols.

Data protocols are responsible for confidentiality and group authentication, should be able to provide source authentication, and ideally replay protection, though that is not always possible because of the complexity of keeping state for multiple senders. Key management protocols must authenticate and authorize members before revealing keys, protect keys in transit, support re-keying if policy sets a lifetime, and revoke membership. Policy protocols must preserve the integrity of the policy, and its confidentiality if the policy is confidential.
sections.eli5: The plan protects the secrets and the rules, but it cannot stop someone from breaking the roads the messages travel on.

items.title: REG
items.text: Unicast SA between the GCKS and each member; protects the other SAs.

items.title: REKEY
items.text: One multicast SA from the GCKS to all members; pushes new SAs and revokes members.
